claim: Bicoid (Bcd) has a central role in anterior-posterior patterning in flies.
source: Here we use ancestral protein reconstruction, biochemical experiments, and developmental assays of transgenic animals carrying reconstructed ancestral genes to investigate how the transcription factor Bicoid (Bcd) evolved its central role in anterior-posterior patterning in flies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the subject of investigation.

claim: Most of Bcd's derived functions are attributable to evolutionary changes within its homeodomain (HD) during a phylogenetic interval >140 million years ago.
source: We show that most of Bcd's derived functions are attributable to evolutionary changes within its homeodomain (HD) during a phylogenetic interval >140 million years ago.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A single substitution Q50K accounts almost entirely for the evolution of Bcd's derived DNA specificity in vitro.
source: A single substitution from this period (Q50K) accounts almost entirely for the evolution of Bcd's derived DNA specificity in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by PBM and EMSA data in the Results section.

claim: In transgenic embryos expressing the reconstructed ancestral HD, Q50K confers activation of only a few of Bcd's transcriptional targets and yields a very partial rescue of anterior development.
source: In transgenic embryos expressing the reconstructed ancestral HD, however, Q50K confers activation of only a few of Bcd's transcriptional targets and yields a very partial rescue of anterior development.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adding a second historical substitution (M54R) confers regulation of additional Bcd targets and further rescues anterior development.
source: Adding a second historical substitution (M54R) confers regulation of additional Bcd targets and further rescues anterior development.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Two epistatically interacting mutations played a major role in the evolution of Bcd's controlling regulatory role in early development.
source: These results indicate that two epistatically interacting mutations played a major role in the evolution of Bcd's controlling regulatory role in early development.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings regarding Q50K and M54R.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster and other cyclorrhaphan flies, AP patterning depends on an anterior gradient of Bicoid (Bcd).
source: In Drosophila melanogaster and other cyclorrhaphan flies – a large taxonomic group that appeared >140 Mya (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005) – AP patterning depends on an anterior gradient of Bicoid (Bcd), a transcription factor translated in the embryo from maternally deposited, anteriorly localized mRNA (Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1988a; Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1988b; Berleth et al., 1988; Little and Wieschaus, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Cyclorrhaphan flies appeared >140 million years ago.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster and other cyclorrhaphan flies – a large taxonomic group that appeared >140 Mya (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grimaldi and Engel, 2005.

claim: Embryos lacking Bcd fail to produce any head or thoracic structures, and duplicate posterior structures are formed in the embryo's anterior.
source: Embryos lacking Bcd fail to produce any head or thoracic structures, and duplicate posterior structures are formed in the embryo's anterior ([Frohnhöfer and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1986]; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1 panels K, L).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to figure panels showing the phenotype.

claim: Bcd directly regulates transcription of dozens of target genes by using its homeodomain (HD) to bind specific cis-regulatory DNA sequences, particularly variants of the canonical motif TAATCC.
source: Bcd directly regulates transcription of dozens of target genes (McGregor et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2012; Driever et al., 1989; Struhl et al., 1989) by using its homeodomain (HD) to bind specific cis-regulatory DNA sequences, particularly variants of the canonical motif TAATCC, with flanking sequences providing some additional specificity (Driever et al., 1989; Struhl et al., 1989; Noyes et al., 2008; Treisman et al., 1989; Dave et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Bcd binds the 3' untranslated region of the messenger RNA of Caudal (Cad) and represses its translation.
source: Bcd also binds the 3' untranslated region of the messenger RNA of Caudal (Cad), a transcription factor involved in development of the posterior end, and represses its translation (Chan and Struhl, 1997; Rivera-Pomar et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In some insect taxa outside the Cyclorrhapha, the gene regulatory network that carries out AP development is similar to that in D. melanogaster, but its anterior deployment is controlled not by Bcd but by other upstream transcription factors.
source: In some insect taxa outside the Cyclorrhapha – such as beetles, wasps, and midges – the gene regulatory network that carries out AP development is similar to that in D. melanogaster, but its anterior deployment is controlled not by Bcd but by other upstream transcription factors (Brent et al., 2007; Klomp et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bcd is unique to cyclorrhaphan flies.
source: Bcd is unique to cyclorrhaphan flies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Bcd's developmental role, anterior localization, and DNA specificity all appear to be derived evolutionary features.
source: Bcd's developmental role, anterior localization, and DNA specificity all appear to be derived evolutionary features, whereas many of Zen's appear to be ancestral (Schmidt-Ott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neither Hox3 nor Zen is anteriorly localized in the embryo or involved in establishing AP polarity.
source: Specifically, neither Hox3 nor Zen is anteriorly localized in the embryo or involved in establishing AP polarity, and both seem to play conserved roles in extraembryonic tissue formation (Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010; van der Zee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both Hox3 and Zen strongly prefer the consensus DNA motif TAATTA over Bcd's TAATCC consensus motif.
source: Both Hox3 and Zen strongly prefer the consensus DNA motif TAATTA over Bcd's TAATCC consensus motif (Noyes et al., 2008; Berger et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neither Hox3 nor Zen regulates Cad translation.
source: and neither regulates Cad translation (Schoppmeier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: K50 is present in several HD proteins that bind canonical target sites similar to Bcd's, but HDs that prefer Zen-like motifs contain a glutamine at this position (Q50).
source: K50 is present in several HD proteins that bind canonical target sites similar to Bcd's, but HDs that prefer Zen-like motifs contain a glutamine at this position (Q50).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on prior biochemical studies.

claim: Biochemical studies have shown that swapping Q50 and K50 between extant HDs affects relative affinity for Bcd-like and Zen-like target sequences.
source: Biochemical studies have shown that swapping these two states between extant HDs affects relative affinity for these target sequences and suggest potential structural mechanisms for this effect (Noyes et al., 2008; Treisman et al., 1989; Ades and Sauer, 1994; Hanes and Brent, 1989; Niessing et al., 2000; Percival-Smith et al., 1990; Schier and Gehring, 1993; Baird-Titus et al., 2006; Otting et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: An arginine at site 54 (R54) has been shown to affect DNA and RNA recognition in vitro.
source: Other residues in the protein's recognition helix, including an arginine at site 54 (R54) have also been shown to affect DNA and RNA recognition in vitro (Dave et al., 2000; Niessing et al., 2000; Hanes and Brent, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Introducing Q50K into D. melanogaster Fushi tarazu (Ftz) does not confer activation of any Bcd targets in fly embryos or cultured cells.
source: The only prior manipulative study to examine the in vivo effects of Q50K on Bcd function introduced this mutation into D. melanogaster Fushi tarazu (Ftz), a distantly related HD protein, and found that Q50K does not confer activation of any Bcd targets in fly embryos (Schier and Gehring, 1993) or cultured cells (Zhao et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Replacing the HD of D. melanogaster Bcd with that of orthodenticle (otd) abolishes activation of most of Bcd's targets and does not rescue anterior development in transgenic embryos.
source: A recent study found that replacing the HD of D. melanogaster Bcd with that of orthodenticle (otd), which also contains K50 and many other sequence differences, abolishes activation of most of Bcd's targets and does not rescue anterior development in transgenic embryos, suggesting that this residue is not sufficient to account for most of the regulatory functions of the Bcd HD (Datta et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The wild-type D. melanogaster Bcd transgene (DmBcd) rescued the bcdE1 phenotype by all molecular and morphological criteria, and over 95% of embryos survived to adulthood.
source: As expected, the wild-type D. melanogaster Bcd transgene (DmBcd) rescued the bcdE1 phenotype by all molecular and morphological criteria, and over 95% of embryos survived to adulthood (Figure 1A–J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-J.

claim: Drosophila Zen (DmZen) failed to rescue any aspect of the bcd-null phenotype.
source: In contrast, Drosophila Zen (DmZen) failed to rescue any aspect of the bcd-null phenotype (Figure 1K–T compared to Figure 1—figure supplement 1K–T).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1K-T.

claim: When DmZen was modified by replacing only its HD with that from D.melanogaster Bcd (DmZen-BcdHD), substantial rescue of morphological and regulatory phenotypes was observed.
source: When DmZen was modified by replacing only its HD with that from D.melanogaster Bcd (DmZen-BcdHD, Figure 1U–DD), we observed substantial rescue of morphological and regulatory phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1U-DD.

claim: A reciprocal construct of the Bcd coding sequence containing the Zen HD (DmBcd-ZenHD) conferred no rescue of any developmental or gene regulatory phenotypes.
source: In contrast, a reciprocal construct of the Bcd coding sequence containing the Zen HD (DmBcd-ZenHD) conferred no rescue of any developmental or gene regulatory phenotypes (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1U–DD).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1U-DD.

claim: Sequence differences within the HD are sufficient to explain a major portion of the Bcd protein's anterior patterning and gene regulatory activities in present-day D. melanogaster embryos.
source: Sequence differences within the HD are therefore sufficient to explain a major portion of the Bcd protein's anterior patterning and gene regulatory activities in present-day D. melanogaster embryos, with much smaller contributions from differences elsewhere in the protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transgenic experiments with HD swaps.

claim: A burst of rapid evolution occurred in the Bcd HD after the duplication, whereas Zen's HD continued to evolve at a slower rate.
source: The phylogenies' branch lengths suggest that a burst of rapid evolution occurred in the Bcd HD after this duplication, whereas Zen's HD continued to evolve at a slower rate (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: AncZB and AncBcd HD differ at 31 amino acid positions.
source: AncZB and AncBcd HD differ at 31 amino acid positions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AncBcd's overall occupancy of DNA motifs was very similar to that of D. melanogaster Bcd (r = 0.94).
source: AncBcd's overall occupancy of DNA motifs was very similar to that of D. melanogaster Bcd (r = 0.94, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on PBM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The correlation between the sequences bound by AncBcd and those bound by AncZB was far weaker (r = 0.56).
source: In contrast, the correlation between the sequences bound by AncBcd and those bound by AncZB was far weaker (r = 0.56, Figure 3B), with thousands of target sequences changing in relative occupancy between AncZB and AncBcd.
evidence: This is based on PBM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Bcd's present-day global specificity is a derived state that evolved on the phylogenetic branch after duplication of AncZB but before the last common ancestor of cyclorrhaphan flies.
source: Bcd's present-day global specificity is therefore a derived state that evolved on the phylogenetic branch after duplication of AncZB but before the last common ancestor of cyclorrhaphan flies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PBM data comparing AncBcd, AncZB, and DmBcd.

claim: AncZB, AncBcd, and DmBcd all share the core consensus motif TAAT (positions 1–4), but with some degeneracy.
source: AncZB, AncBcd, and DmBcd all share the core consensus motif TAAT (positions 1–4), but with some degeneracy.
evidence: This is based on energy logos derived from PBM data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The major differences in DNA binding between AncZB and AncBcd/DmBcd are at positions 5 and 6: AncZB prefers T or G at position 5 and A or G at position 6, but AncBcd and DmBcd strongly prefer sequences containing CC at these two positions.
source: The major differences are at positions 5 and 6: AncZB prefers T or G at position 5 and A or G at position 6 (Figure 3C), but AncBcd and DmBcd strongly prefer sequences containing CC at these two positions (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is based on energy logos derived from PBM data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Relative preference for Bcd motifs increased dramatically across the interval from AncZB and AncBcd, with affinity for BM increasing 25-fold and that for ZM declining by a factor of 10.
source: We found that relative preference for Bcd motifs increased dramatically across the interval from AncZB and AncBcd, with affinity for BM increasing 25-fold and that for ZM declining by a factor of 10 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on F-EMSA data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Changes in affinity between AncZB and AncBcd were caused primarily by changes in dissociation rates: AncBcd's off-rate from BM was 66-fold slower than AncZB's, and its off-rate from ZM was three times faster.
source: Changes in affinity were caused primarily by changes in dissociation rates: AncBcd's off-rate from BM was 66-fold slower than AncZB's, and its off-rate from ZM was three times faster; changes in on-rates were small (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on SPR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Between AncZB and AncBcd, residence time on BM increased by 70-fold, while that on ZM declined by a factor of 3.
source: As a result, there was a strong evolutionary shift in average residence times on the two motifs: between AncZB and AncBcd, residence time on BM increased by 70-fold, while that on ZM declined by a factor of 3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on SPR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 4.

claim: The reconstructed AncBcd HD yielded a phenotype indistinguishable from that of the DmBcd transgene, with essentially complete morphological rescue, activation of all Bcd targets, and repression of Cad, with 37% of embryos surviving to adulthood.
source: The reconstructed AncBcd HD yielded a phenotype indistinguishable from that of the DmBcd transgene, with essentially complete morphological rescue (Figure 3G,H), activation of all Bcd targets (Figure 3J–P), and repression of Cad (Figure 3I), with 37% of embryos surviving to adulthood.
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 3G-P.

claim: When the AncZB HD was swapped into the DmBcd construct, no morphological or molecular rescue was observed.
source: In contrast, when the AncZB HD was swapped into the same construct, no morphological or molecular rescue was observed (Figure 3Q–Z).
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 3Q-Z.

claim: The derived in vivo functions of the Bcd homeodomain evolved almost entirely during the interval after duplication of AncZB but before AncBcd.
source: The derived in vivo functions of the Bcd homeodomain – including its capacity to regulate key developmental target genes and to specify formation of cephalic and thoracic structures in anterior regions of the embryo – therefore evolved almost entirely during the interval after duplication of AncZB but before AncBcd.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transgenic experiments with AncBcd and AncZB HDs.

claim: Eleven of the 31 amino acid substitutions that occurred between AncZB and AncBcd are phylogenetically diagnostic, with the AncBcd state conserved in all descendant Bcd proteins.
source: Eleven of the 31 amino acid substitutions that occurred between AncZB and AncBcd are phylogenetically diagnostic, with the AncBcd state conserved in all descendant Bcd proteins (Figure 2B); these diagnostic substitutions constitute an initial set of candidate causal changes.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only one reversal – changing lysine 50 back to the ancestral glutamine (K50q) – shifted the protein's preference for BM back toward ZM; this reversion caused a 38-fold change in relative affinity and restored the ancestral preference for ZM.
source: Only one reversal – changing lysine 50 back to the ancestral glutamine (K50q) – shifted the protein's preference for BM back toward ZM; this reversion caused a 38-fold change in relative affinity and restored the ancestral preference for ZM.
evidence: This is based on F-EMSA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutating arginine (R) to the ancestral methionine (m) at position 54 (R54m) had no effect on relative preference, but it lowered affinity to both BM and ZM by a factor of ~15.
source: Mutating arginine (R) to the ancestral methionine (m) at position 54 (R54m) – had no effect on relative preference, but it lowered affinity to both BM and ZM by a factor of ~15 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on F-EMSA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Substitution q50K was sufficient to cause the entire historical shift in in vitro DNA preference from ZM to BM.
source: Substitution q50K had a very large effect, shifting the ancestral protein's relative binding preference by four orders of magnitude, increasing affinity for BM 100-fold and reducing that for ZM by a factor of 100 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on F-EMSA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Simultaneously introducing into AncZB all 30 other substitutions from this interval except q50K (construct AncBcd-K50q) caused no improvement in affinity for BM and just a seven-fold reduction in affinity to ZM.
source: By comparison, simultaneously introducing into AncZB all 30 other substitutions from this interval except q50K (construct AncBcd-K50q) caused no improvement in affinity for BM and just a seven-fold reduction in affinity to ZM (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on F-EMSA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Substitution m54R alone increased affinity for both ZM and BM, but in the presence of q50K, it had no significant effect, indicating an epistatic interaction by which q50K silences the effect of m54R.
source: Substitution m54R alone increased affinity for both ZM and BM, but in the presence of q50K, it had no significant effect, indicating an epistatic interaction by which q50K silences the effect of m54R (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on F-EMSA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The single substitution q50K was sufficient to cause the entire historical shift in in vitro DNA preference from ZM to BM, whereas m54R did not make an observable contribution to the new specificity.
source: These data indicate that the single substitution q50K was sufficient to cause the entire historical shift in in vitro DNA preference from ZM to BM, whereas m54R did not make an observable contribution to the new specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the F-EMSA data in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Substitution q50K shifted the overall enrichment and de-enrichment across all oligomers to be extremely similar to those bound by AncBcd (r = 0.93).
source: This substitution shifted the overall enrichment and de-enrichment across all oligomers to be extremely similar to those bound by AncBcd (Figure 4C, r = 0.93, compared to r = 0.56 for the correlation of AncZB and AncBcd (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on PBM data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Substitution q50K transformed the binding-energy logo of AncZB into one almost identical to that of AncBcd, with the 'CC' dinucleotide strongly favored at positions 5 and 6.
source: Substitution q50K also transformed the binding-energy logo of AncZB into one almost identical to that of AncBcd, with the 'CC' dinucleotide strongly favored at positions 5 and 6 and the ancestrally preferred bases now de-enriched (Figure 4D, compared to Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on PBM data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Substitution q50K was the primary determinant of the evolutionary shift in in vitro DNA-binding preferences that occurred during the transition from AncZB to AncBcd.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that substitution q50K was the primary determinant of the evolutionary shift in in vitro DNA-binding preferences that occurred during the transition from AncZB to AncBcd.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PBM and F-EMSA data in Figure 4.

claim: The other 30 substitutions that occurred on this branch, including m54R, had very minor effects on the in vitro DNA-binding specificity of the evolving HD.
source: The other 30 substitutions that occurred on this branch, including m54R, had very minor effects on the in vitro DNA-binding specificity of the evolving HD.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PBM and F-EMSA data in Figure 4.

claim: Reversing only q50K (AncBcdHD-K50q) completely abolished the rescue conferred by AncBcd HD: larval cuticles were similar to bcd-null embryos, expression of Bcd's transcriptional targets was completely lost, and Cad translation was no longer repressed.
source: We found that reversing only q50K (AncBcdHD-K50q) completely abolished the rescue conferred by AncBcd HD: larval cuticles were similar to bcd-null embryos (Figure 5A,B), expression of Bcd's transcriptional targets was completely lost (Figure 5D–J), and Cad translation was no longer repressed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5A-J.

claim: Substitution q50K was necessary for evolution of the developmental and gene regulatory functions of the Bcd HD.
source: Substitution q50K was therefore necessary for evolution of the developmental and gene regulatory functions of the Bcd HD.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5A-J.

claim: Introducing the derived lysine into the AncZB HD (q50K) resulted in partial rescue: ectopic filzkörper formation was suppressed, and all eight abdominal segments were formed in ~90% of the embryos.
source: We observed partial rescue (Figure 5K–T). Ectopic filzkörper formation was suppressed, and all eight abdominal segments were formed in ~90% of the embryos (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5K-T and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Embryos with AncZB HD plus q50K failed to form anterior thoracic segments (T1 and T2) and any head structures.
source: These embryos failed to form anterior thoracic segments (T1 and T2) and any head structures (Figure 5K,L, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5K-L and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Of Bcd's seven transcriptional targets, three (hb, kni, and eve stripe 2) were activated by AncZB HD plus q50K, but four (gt, otd, ems, and btd) were not.
source: Of Bcd's seven transcriptional targets, three (hb, kni, and eve stripe 2) were activated, but four (gt, otd, ems, and btd) were not (Figure 5N–T), and Cad translation was not repressed (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5M-T.

claim: q50K partially accounts for the evolution of Bcd's role in development and gene regulation in vivo.
source: Thus, q50K partially accounts for the evolution of Bcd's role in development and gene regulation in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5K-T.

claim: Introducing m54R alone into AncZB HD conferred no observable rescue of developmental or gene regulatory phenotypes.
source: Introducing m54R alone into AncZB HD conferred no observable rescue of developmental or gene regulatory phenotypes (Figure 5U–DD).
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5U-DD.

claim: Introducing m54R together with q50K yielded a notably more complete rescue than q50K alone: all larvae carrying the double substitution contained T3 and all eight abdominal segments, >80% also contained T2, and >50% formed anterior structures similar to the sclerotized structures of the internal cephalic skeleton.
source: Introducing m54R together with q50K, however, yielded a notably more complete rescue than q50K alone: all larvae carrying the double substitution contained T3 and all eight abdominal segments,>80% also contained T2, and >50% formed anterior structures similar to the sclerotized structures of the internal cephalic skeleton (Figure 5EE,FF; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5EE-FF and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Compared to the single q50K substitution, two additional Bcd-dependent transcriptional targets, gt and otd, were activated by the double substitution q50K/m54R.
source: Compared to the single q50K substitution, two additional Bcd-dependent transcriptional targets, gt and otd, were activated (Figure 5HH–KK,NN), but two others, btd and ems, remained silent (Figure 5LL,MM), and Cad translation was still not repressed in the anterior (Figure 5GG).
evidence: This is based on transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5GG-NN.

claim: There is an epistatic interaction between m54R and q50K in vivo, in which m54R has an effect only when introduced together with q50K.
source: These data point to an epistatic interaction between m54R and q50K in vivo, in which m54R has an effect only when introduced together with q50K; this interaction differs from that observed in vitro, where m54R affects affinity in isolation but not in combination with q50K.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the transgenic experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Just two large-effect substitutions – q50K and m54R – are sufficient in the ancestral HD to recapitulate the evolution of major aspects of the Bcd HD's derived function, including regulation of many target genes and partial specification of anterior structures.
source: Thus, just two large-effect substitutions – q50K and m54R – are sufficient in the ancestral HD to recapitulate the evolution of major aspects of the Bcd HD's derived function, including regulation of many target genes and partial specification of anterior structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transgenic experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Compared to the phenotype of AncBcd-HD, the rescue conferred by q50K and m54R is incomplete, with several targets remaining unregulated and anterior development still compromised.
source: Compared to the phenotype of AncBcd-HD, the rescue conferred by these two substitutions is incomplete, with several targets remaining unregulated and anterior development still compromised.
evidence: This is based on comparing the transgenic experiments in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Additional contributions must have been made by some of the other historical substitutions in the HD during the interval between AncZB and AncBcd.
source: Additional contributions must therefore have been made by some of the other historical substitutions in the HD during the interval between AncZB and AncBcd.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue by q50K and m54R compared to AncBcd.

claim: The difference observed between the in vitro and in vivo contributions of the key historical substitutions indicates that the evolution of Bcd's developmental functions cannot be explained entirely by a shift in binding to canonical ZM and BM.
source: The difference we observed between the in vitro and in vivo contributions of the key historical substitutions indicates that the evolution of Bcd's developmental functions cannot be explained entirely by a shift in binding to canonical ZM and BM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: Q50K causes the entire shift in preference measured in vitro, but it accounts for a relatively small portion of the HD's in vivo evolution – activation of three of seven major transcriptional target genes, and only a very limited rescue of anterior development.
source: Q50K causes the entire shift in preference measured in vitro, but it accounts for a relatively small portion of the HD's in vivo evolution – activation of three of seven major transcriptional target genes, and only a very limited rescue of anterior development; two of these, hb and eve2, are the same targets that are activated by a construct of the D. melanogaster bcd gene containing the otd HD, which also contains K50 (Datta et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vitro and in vivo results, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Adding M54R to Q50K had no further effect on preference or affinity in vitro, but it conferred a notably more complete rescue in vivo.
source: Adding M54R to Q50K had no further effect on preference or affinity in vitro, but it conferred a notably more complete rescue in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The AncZB-Q50K/M54R construct showed no detectable inhibition of Cad in vivo, indicating that M54R's effects are mediated by some other mechanism.
source: Residue Arg54 has been proposed to be critical for Cad inhibition (Niessing et al., 2000), but the AncZB-Q50K/M54R construct showed no detectable inhibition of Cad in vivo, indicating that M54R's effects are mediated by some other mechanism.
evidence: This is based on the transgenic experiments shown in Figure 5GG and a citation to prior work.

claim: RNAs from all transgenes were anteriorly localized in a fashion indistinguishable from the endogenous bcd mRNA pattern.
source: RNAs from all transgenes were anteriorly localized in a fashion indistinguishable from the endogenous bcd mRNA pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 1EE-GG).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1EE-GG.

claim: Both AncZB and AncBcd HD sequences are reconstructed with little statistical ambiguity (mean posterior probability = 0.970 and 0.986, with only 3 and 2 sites ambiguously reconstructed in AncZB and AncBcd, respectively).
source: Both sequences are reconstructed with little statistical ambiguity (mean posterior probability = 0.970 and 0.986, with only 3 and 2 sites ambiguously reconstructed in AncZB and AncBcd, respectively (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the ancestral sequence reconstruction analysis.

claim: PBMs performed using alternative reconstructions of AncBcd and AncZB yielded almost identical results to the maximum likelihood reconstructions.
source: These findings were robust to uncertainty about the sequences of the ancestral HDs: PBMs performed using alternative reconstructions of AncBcd and AncZB, which incorporated plausible alternative amino acid states at all ambiguously reconstructed sites (Eick et al., 2017), yielded almost identical results (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on PBM data using alternative reconstructions.

claim: Alternative reconstructions of AncZB and AncBcd HDs yielded nearly identical results in F-EMSA experiments.
source: Alternative reconstructions of AncZB and AncBcd HDs yielded nearly identical results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on F-EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
